source.title: Assessment of gastrocnemius tensiomyographic neuromuscular characteristics as risk factors for anterior cruciate ligament injury in male soccer players

paper.citation: Alentorn-Geli, E., Alvarez-Diaz, P., Ramon, S., Marin, M., Steinbacher, G., Rius, M., Seijas, R., Ares, O., & Cugat, R. (2015). Assessment of gastrocnemius tensiomyographic neuromuscular characteristics as risk factors for anterior cruciate ligament injury in male soccer players. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy, 23(9), 2502–2507. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00167-014-3007-4
paper.abstract: Do resting medial and lateral gastrocnemius TMG characteristics differ between male soccer players with ACL rupture and matched uninjured controls? Forty male competitive soccer players with complete primary ACL tear and 38 sex- and sport-level-matched healthy controls. TMG was measured at rest on the uninjured limb before surgery and compared with the bilateral mean of controls. Soccer, male, injured-case context; transfer to prospective collegiate American-football screening is indirect. Cross-sectional controlled comparison, despite the paper's risk-factor framing. TMG measured maximal displacement plus delay, contraction, sustained, and half-relaxation times in medial and lateral gastrocnemius. Independent t tests compared groups; planned sample size was approximately 35–36 per group.
paper.tldr: This paper informs whether resting gastrocnemius tensiomyography can be interpreted as an ACL-risk marker. Most TMG variables did not differ between groups; medial-gastrocnemius half-relaxation time was 71.5 ± 52.7 versus 53.2 ± 35.3 ms (p = 0.02). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional controlled comparison, despite the paper's risk-factor framing. TMG measured maximal displacement plus delay, contraction, sustained, and half-relaxation times in medial and lateral gastrocnemius. Independent t tests compared groups; planned sample size was approximately 35–36 per group.
paper.findings: Most TMG variables did not differ between groups; medial-gastrocnemius half-relaxation time was 71.5 ± 52.7 versus 53.2 ± 35.3 ms (p = 0.02). Medial-gastrocnemius maximal displacement was 3.7 ± 1.4 versus 3.1 ± 1.0 mm (p = 0.006); other medial and lateral gastrocnemius variables were nonsignificant.
paper.limitations: These postinjury cross-sectional differences cannot establish preinjury risk or predictive accuracy. Static resting measurements differ materially from on-field cutting and landing. ACL injury may itself alter the contralateral limb, creating reverse-causation risk. Soleus was not assessed, and reliability had not been established specifically for gastrocnemius medialis/lateralis. Multiple variable testing without a reported multiplicity correction increases false-positive concern.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use these resting gastrocnemius TMG measures as an ACL-risk screen. At most, they are exploratory postinjury characteristics requiring prospective validation, known measurement error, and sport-specific dynamic outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Do not use these resting gastrocnemius TMG measures as an ACL-risk screen. At most, they are exploratory postinjury characteristics requiring prospective validation, known measurement error, and sport-specific dynamic outcomes. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, do not use these resting gastrocnemius TMG measures as an ACL-risk screen. At most, they are exploratory postinjury characteristics requiring prospective validation, known measurement error, and sport-specific dynamic outcomes. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
